questions.stem: A naive CD4+ T cell differentiates into the subset shown, which secretes IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and drives IgE class switching, mast cell degranulation, eosinophil activation, and intestinal mucus/peristalsis. This response is MOST important for host defense against which of the following?

explanation.summary: The figure depicts Th2 differentiation and its effector arms (IL-4/5/13, IgE, eosinophils, mast cells, mucus and peristalsis). This program mediates immunity against helminths and, when dysregulated, causes allergic disease. Intracellular pathogens are handled by Th1/CD8 responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure depicts Th2 differentiation and its effector arms (IL-4/5/13, IgE, eosinophils, mast cells, mucus and peristalsis). This program mediates immunity against helminths and, when dysregulated, causes allergic disease. Intracellular pathogens are handled by Th1/CD8 responses.

questions.stem: The CD4+ Th1 cell activates the macrophage via CD40L-CD40 and IFN-gamma. What is the principal antimicrobial consequence of this activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgE class switching in B cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct antibody-mediated pore formation in bacteria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enhanced killing of phagocytosed intracellular microbes

explanation.summary: Th1 cells license macrophages through CD40L-CD40 and IFN-gamma. The activated ('classically activated') macrophage generates ROS and NO to kill ingested microbes, secretes TNF/IL-1/IL-12, and upregulates MHC and B7.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th1 cells license macrophages through CD40L-CD40 and IFN-gamma. The activated ('classically activated') macrophage generates ROS and NO to kill ingested microbes, secretes TNF/IL-1/IL-12, and upregulates MHC and B7.

questions.stem: The CD8+ T cell kills the virus-infected cell using the receptor-ligand pair and downstream caspase shown, without releasing cytotoxic granules. This represents which of the following?

explanation.summary: FasL on the CTL engages Fas on the target, activating caspase-3 and apoptosis. This death-receptor pathway is an alternative to perforin/granzyme granule exocytosis and does not require granule contents.
explanation.whyCorrect: FasL on the CTL engages Fas on the target, activating caspase-3 and apoptosis. This death-receptor pathway is an alternative to perforin/granzyme granule exocytosis and does not require granule contents.

questions.stem: A CD8+ cytotoxic T cell recognizes a virus-infected cell via MHC I and releases the granule contents shown. What is the specific role of perforin in this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It forms pores in the target-cell membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: It cross-links Fas to trigger caspases

choices.label: E
choices.text: It fixes complement on the target membrane

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic granules contain perforin, granzymes, and serglycin. Perforin polymerizes to create pores that let granzymes enter the cytosol, where they activate caspases and induce apoptosis of the infected cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytotoxic granules contain perforin, granzymes, and serglycin. Perforin polymerizes to create pores that let granzymes enter the cytosol, where they activate caspases and induce apoptosis of the infected cell.

questions.stem: An antibody-coated tumor cell is recognized by the CD16 Fc receptor on the effector cell shown; Fc cross-linking triggers degranulation and the target dies by apoptosis. What is this killing mechanism called?

explanation.summary: NK cells express CD16 (FcγRIII), which binds the Fc region of IgG coating a target cell. Cross-linking triggers release of cytotoxic granules, killing the antibody-coated cell by ADCC. This differs from complement lysis and from phagocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: NK cells express CD16 (FcγRIII), which binds the Fc region of IgG coating a target cell. Cross-linking triggers release of cytotoxic granules, killing the antibody-coated cell by ADCC. This differs from complement lysis and from phagocytosis.
